title: Neurologic Diseases and Opportunistic Infections in HIV

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of fevers, headache, and gradually increasing confusion. The patient was known to have HIV and a history of nonadherence to her antiretroviral therapy. On physical exam, the patient appeared somnolent but had no focal neurologic deficits. A CT head and a lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: Noncontrasted CT of the head: normal appearances CD4 count 85 cells/μL HIV viral load 450 copies/mL Serum cryptococcal antigen positive 1:128 Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 mmHg CSF WBC count 4/mm3, CSF glucose 30 mg/dL (45–80) CSF total protein 110 mg/dL (20–40) CSF Gram stain negative CSF cryptococcal antigen positive 1:32
questions.lead_in: In addition to starting antifungal therapy, what therapeutic intervention is warranted?
questions.explanation: Serial lumbar punctures The patient has presented with cryptococcal meningitis and evidence of elevated intracranial pressures (ICP). Unlike some other causes of elevation in the ICP , pharmacologic management with either acetazolamide, dexamethasone, or mannitol is not effective in cryptococcal meningitis. The first-line treatment is serial large-volume lumbar punctures to reduce the elevated ICP . Neurosurgical interventions such as lumbar drain placement, ventriculostomy, or VP shunting are reserved for refractory cases or in patients with evidence of imminent herniation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q23

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with new-onset neurologic deficits. He reported having mental slowing, with poor concentration and memory loss. As an example, he reported getting lost when driving to his home of 20 years. He was known to have HIV and was taking antiretroviral therapy. Neurologic examination was normal. A CT head and lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: CD4 count 760 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable CT head without contrast: normal CSF white cell count 6 ×106/L CSF HIV viral load 12,588 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most important diagnostic test to guide management?

options.text: B12, thyroid function, and syphilis screen
HIV genotyping of the CSF virus

questions.explanation: HIV genotyping of the CSF virus CNS viral escape syndrome is an uncommon condition that can be seen in patients with HIV on ART . It is defined by presence of CNS HIV replication in CSF despite viral suppression or low-grade viremia. New-onset neurocognitive symptoms may range from HIV-associated dementia to focal neurologic deficits. CSF pleocytosis is often present with a CD8 predominance. Clinical management should include assessment of the CSF genotype due to compartmentalized resistant virus that may be present in the CSF . If found, ART regimens should be changed based on CSF genotype results. A nerve conduction study would be used to evaluate for neuropathies. HIV-associated peripheral neuropathies are common in persons with advanced disease (CD4 cell counts <200 cells/ μL). They are usually distal symmetrical neuropathies. Several drugs may also be associated with development of peripheral neuropathies, particularly older protease inhibitors (i.e., indinavir, saquinavir, and ritonavir). This may also be caused by drugs used to treat opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses, like dapsone, vincristine, isoniazid, and ethambutol. Initiation of ART is recommended to reduce the risk of developing distal symmetric polyneuropathy, but it is unclear if it can reduce severity of already present disease. Symptomatic management with pharmacotherapy is recommended such as gabapentin and potentially secondline regimens like a tricyclic antidepressant and topical capsaicin. MRI are typically recommended to evaluate patients where HIV-associated dementia is a concern with severe deficits to rule out other common neurologic disorders like neoplasms or infections. Also, while MRI is typically included in the evaluation of a patient with neurocognitive decline and suppressed viral load, it would not guide management in this case. HIV-associated dementia almost exclusively is seen in persons who have not initiated ART with advanced disease (CD4 cell count <200 cells/ μL). Lumbar punctures may also be done when evaluating a patient with advanced disease and neurocognitive deficits to rule out other etiologies. However, CSF HIV RNA levels would not be diagnostic of HAD, and typically an elevated CSF protein and red blood cells may be seen. B12 deficiency, thyroid function, and syphilis should all be considered in a patient with dementia but are unlikely to have been undetected in a patient who has been under routine HIV care for a prolonged period.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive right arm weakness and a 1-week history of increasing confusion and word-finding difficulties. He was known to have HIV , and although previously on ART he had been lost to clinical care and follow-up 3 years earlier. On physical exam, neurologic exam was notable for 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and an expressive aphasia. Investigations: MRI of the brain: there are multiple discrete lesions in the cortical white matter and basal ganglia, which are hyperintense on the T2-weighted imaging sequences. CD4 count 125 cells/μL HIV viral load 45,200 copies/mL Serum RPR negative Serum cryptococcal antigen negative Toxoplasma IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy The most likely diagnosis given the clinical syndrome and characteristic findings on MRI of the brain is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus. The recommended treatment for PML is immediate initiation of ART to achieve immune reconstitution. Treatments such as cidofovir, cytarabine, and 5HT2a serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as mirtazapine have been tested but have shown no or inconclusive clinical benefit. The antivirals aciclovir and ganciclovir do not have activity against JC virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q22

questions.question: Lumbar puncture in the patient with HIV.

parts.text: Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

parts_raw.text: 12. Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Suspected meningitis/encephalitis: fever, headache, meningismus, seizure or altered level of consciousness (cryptococcal, tuberculous, bacterial, CMV, HSV/VZV). (2) Syphilis with neurologic, ocular or otic symptoms, or serologic failure (RPR not falling four-fold after treatment). (3) Positive serum cryptococcal antigen with CD4 <100 (to exclude meningitis), and therapeutic/diagnostic taps for elevated CSF opening pressure in cryptococcal meningitis. (4) Undiagnosed intracranial lesions or white-matter disease needing CSF PCR/cytology - JC virus for PML, EBV for primary CNS lymphoma - or new/progressive neurocognitive decline with suspected CSF viral escape.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS/NIH OI guidelines and CDC STI 2021 supply the specific neurosyphilis LP triggers and CrAg screening threshold.

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis with focal neuro deficits/altered LOC; syphilis with failure to improve RPR dilutions as expected; HIV with neurocognitive concern/possible HIV dementia; cryptococcal meningitis with features of elevated ICP; failure of virologic suppression; intracranial abnormality on imaging; any concern for meningitis/encephalitis with altered LOC

questions.question: A woman with HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure and focal neurologic deficits. CT head shows 3 large gray matter lesions, the largest about 3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.
questions.question_raw: 18. A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.
questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load, then 50 mg/day (<60 kg) or 75 mg/day (>=60 kg), PLUS sulfadiazine 1000 mg (<60 kg) or 1500 mg (>=60 kg) q6h, PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy 3-6 weeks then maintenance. b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) the same pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid regimen is acceptable (pyrimethamine avoided only in first trimester); alternative pyrimethamine-clindamycin-folinic acid. c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

cohort_answer.text: 1st line: Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 dose then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Septra 10mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV/PO divided q12h. If <60kg, Sulfadiazine dose 1g QID. Pregnant (16 weeks): Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Leucovorin. Alternative diagnosis: CNS lymphoma; also MTB, Cryptococcus.

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load, then 50-75 mg/day, PLUS sulfadiazine 1000-1500 mg q6h, PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy 3-6 weeks then maintenance until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART. b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) the same pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid regimen can be used (pyrimethamine avoided only in the first trimester). c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND).
questions.model_answer: a) A spectrum of cognitive, motor and behavioural impairment attributable to HIV infection of the central nervous system once other causes are excluded, graded as asymptomatic neurocognitive impairment, mild neurocognitive disorder, and HIV-associated dementia. HIV enters the CNS early via trafficking infected monocytes/lymphocytes and is sustained in perivascular macrophages and microglia, producing immune activation and neuronal injury rather than direct neuronal infection. Clinically: memory and attention impairment, psychomotor slowing, apathy and social withdrawal, gait instability and impaired fine motor control. Risk factors include low nadir CD4 count, older age, and vascular/metabolic comorbidity. Antiretroviral therapy has largely eliminated severe dementia but milder forms persist despite virologic suppression. Investigations: MRI shows atrophy with symmetric non-enhancing periventricular T2 hyperintensity (no T1 hypointensity, unlike PML), and CSF may show mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.

cohort_answer.text: Changes in memory, concentration, attention, motor skills common in HIV, without evident cause other than HIV, classified as HAND (ANI, MND, HAD). ART use decreased prevalence of severe deficits (HAD) but milder deficits remain common even with viral suppression. Risk factors: low nadir CD4, age, comorbidities (CV, metabolic). Dysfunction does not reverse with ART. Pathophys: early infection of CNS via trafficking lymphocytes, then autonomous infection of CNS monocytes/macrophages. Subtle sx: memory defects, slow thinking, trouble concentrating, apathy, social withdrawal, decreased coordination, altered writing, loss of balance/gait instability. Investigations: subtle EEG changes, CSF mild lymphopleocytosis/elevated protein, MRI greater subcortical than cortical atrophy, multiple hyperintense T2 lesions non-enhancing, no T1 intensity (distinguished from PML)

questions.question: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND).
questions.model_answer: a) Start or optimize antiretroviral therapy to achieve plasma virologic suppression - the primary intervention, though it stabilizes more often than reverses deficits. Systematically exclude and treat alternative or contributing causes: opportunistic CNS infection (cryptococcus, syphilis, PML, CMV, TB), CNS lymphoma, depression, substance use, medication effects (including efavirenz), thyroid and B12 deficiency, and vascular/metabolic disease. If deficits progress despite plasma suppression, perform an LP for CSF HIV RNA and resistance testing to identify CSF viral escape, and tailor the regimen accordingly. Manage comorbid cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors, and provide neuropsychological assessment, rehabilitation, cognitive and functional supports, and adherence assistance. No adjunctive neuroprotective agent has shown proven benefit.

cohort_answer.text: ART, although minimally effective in reversing HAND. In case of 'CNS viral escape' consider regimen with higher CSF penetration (PI based regimens associated with greater odds of CNS viral escape). Rule out other reversible etiologies and contributing factors. Non-pharmacological strategies

questions.question: A 15-year-old with HIV, poorly controlled and off antiretrovirals, presents with focal neurologic signs, seizures, and ring-enhancing lesions. He had Stevens-Johnson syndrome to co-trimoxazole (septra) previously and is not on prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: 15 year old with HIV, poorly controlled off ARVs. Comes in with focal neurological signs and seizures, ring enhancing lesions. Had SJS to septra previously. Not on ppx.

parts.text: Treatment, and when to stop secondary prophylaxis.

parts_raw.text: B) Treatment, when to stop secondary ppx

questions.model_answer: a) CNS toxoplasmosis (toxoplasmic encephalitis). b) Because of the sulfa allergy, use pyrimethamine (200 mg load, then 50-75 mg/day) plus clindamycin (600 mg q6h) plus folinic acid for at least 3-6 weeks, followed by secondary suppression (same agents at reduced dose); add separate PCP prophylaxis (e.g., atovaquone) as clindamycin-pyrimethamine lacks anti-Pneumocystis activity. Stop secondary prophylaxis once CD4 >200 cells/mm3 is sustained for at least 6 months on ART with resolution of signs/symptoms.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer says to stop secondary prophylaxis after CD4 >200 for >3 months; Mandell specifies a sustained CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART.

cohort_answer.text:
CNS toxoplasmosis
Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin (+leucovorin/folinic acid) x6 weeks then secondary suppression. Stop secondary ppx once CD4 >200 on ARVs for >3 months, no further signs/sx of toxo encephalopathy. Secondary ppx for septra allergy: Atovaquone

questions.question: A patient with HIV has white matter lesions with no mass effect. Complete a table of pathogen or cause and the associated disease.
questions.question_raw: A patient with HIV has white matter lesions with no mass effect. Fill in the table below: Pathogen/Cause | Associated Disease

parts.text: Fill in pathogen and associated disease for white matter lesions with no mass effect (four entries).

parts_raw.text: Fill in pathogen and associated disease for white matter lesions with no mass effect (4 entries)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. (2) HIV-1 - HIV encephalopathy/HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HIV leukoencephalopathy). (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningoencephalitis (basal meningitis with infarcts). Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis with dilated perivascular spaces is an acceptable alternative.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer lists tuberculomas, cryptococcomas and toxoplasmomas; these are mass lesions and do not fit a question specifying white-matter lesions without mass effect.

cohort_answer.text: JC | PML. TB | TB encephalitis, tuberculoma. Crypto | Crypto encephalitis, cryptococcomas. Toxo | Toxo encephalitis, toxoplasmomas.

questions.question: Lumbar puncture in the patient with HIV.
questions.question_raw: 12. Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

parts.text: Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

parts_raw.text: Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Suspected meningitis or encephalitis - fever, headache, meningismus, seizure or altered level of consciousness - to evaluate for cryptococcal, tuberculous, bacterial, CMV or HSV/VZV disease. (2) Syphilis with neurologic, ocular or otic symptoms, or failure of the RPR to fall four-fold after appropriate therapy. (3) Cryptococcal disease: a positive serum cryptococcal antigen with CD4 <100 to exclude meningitis, and repeat therapeutic taps for elevated opening pressure during treatment. (4) Undiagnosed intracranial lesions or unexplained neurocognitive decline requiring CSF studies - JC virus PCR for PML, EBV DNA and cytology for primary CNS lymphoma, and CSF HIV RNA for suspected CSF viral escape.

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis (neurologic manifestations with positive serology; asymptomatic syphilis when CD4<350 and RPR>1:32; RPR not downtrending despite treatment). Cryptococcus (therapeutic tap to reduce CSF pressure; CD4<100 and screening serum CrAg positive). Suspected PML (JC virus PCR from LP). Suspected CNS lymphoma. Meningismus/Encephalitis (after CT, blood cultures, and antibiotics started per IDSA 2004 guidelines) - Cryptococcus, TB, CMV. Concern for CSF virologic escape. Toxoplasmosis - LP for T gondii PCR, cytology, culture, CrAg, MTB, EBV, JC virus (DHHS guidelines).

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with HIV, CD4 count 50 cells/uL, non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy, presents with ataxia and vague neurologic symptoms and no headache. No focal deficits on examination. No travel history; lives in Toronto. No lumbar puncture performed. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.
questions.question_raw: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give four pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

parts_raw.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: multifocal non-enhancing white-matter lesions without mass effect, ataxia, hemiparesis, visual and cognitive decline. (2) HIV-1 itself - HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder/HIV encephalopathy: symmetric periventricular white-matter change with atrophy, psychomotor slowing, gait instability. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis (also polyradiculomyelitis): periventricular enhancement, confusion, cranial neuropathies at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningitis with basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas and infarcts. (Also consider Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma, though both typically show ring enhancement and mass effect.)

questions.question: A man with HIV who has lived in Toronto his entire life is non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 count of 50 cells/uL. He presents with three weeks of altered level of consciousness and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the four most likely organisms and the diseases they cause?

parts_raw.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (asymmetric, non-enhancing white-matter lesions, no mass effect; diagnosis by CSF JC virus PCR). (2) HIV-1 - HIV encephalopathy/HIV-associated dementia with diffuse symmetric white-matter signal change and atrophy. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningoencephalitis with basal meningitis and infarction. Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis is the other key consideration; Toxoplasma encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma are less likely given the absence of mass effect.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists HSV and VZV as leading answers; in advanced HIV with subacute multifocal white-matter disease and no mass effect, PML, HIV encephalopathy, CMV and tuberculosis are the higher-yield answers.

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

parts.text: Man from Toronto with HIV with CD4 50, 3 weeks worsening ataxia and difficulty concentrating and memory loss, probably other symptoms, no focal neuro though. MRI shows no space occupying lesions but does show multifocal white matter disease. What are four organisms implicated and the diseases they cause?

parts_raw.text: Man from Toronto with HIV with CD4 50, 3 weeks worsening ataxia and difficulty concentrating and memory loss, probably other symptoms, no focal neuro though. MRI shows no space occupying lesions but does show multifocal white matter disease. What are four organisms implicated and the diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (asymmetric non-enhancing subcortical white matter lesions, the leading diagnosis here). (2) HIV itself - HIV encephalopathy / HIV-associated leukoencephalopathy. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis. (4) Epstein-Barr virus - primary CNS lymphoma (though typically mass-forming/enhancing).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only JCV/PML is covered by this Mandell chapter; the HIV, CMV, and EBV differentials for multifocal white-matter disease in advanced AIDS are from the broader HIV CNS opportunistic-infection literature (Mandell HIV/CNS chapters).
